item.title: AUDUSD retraces some of the gains seen yesterday. What next for traders?
item.description:
The AUDUSD has been on a rollercoaster ride this week, with sharp swings in both directions. The week began with the pair trading below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages. Sellers then pushed the price below a trendline and a key swing area, sending it toward the 200-day moving average, but the decline stalled before that longer-term target could be reached.

Momentum then shifted dramatically. Helped by the FOMC reaction, the sharp decline in the USDJPY, broad U.S. dollar selling, and stronger equity markets, the AUDUSD rebounded aggressively. The pair climbed back above its 100- and 200-hour moving averages, tilting the short-term bias back to the upside, and extended above the 38.2% retracement of the decline from the May high to the late-June low at 0.7022. The rally reached 0.70435, stopping just 9 pips shy of the 100-day moving average at 0.7052.

Today's trading has brought another twist. Renewed dollar buying pushed the pair lower, but sellers were unable to force a break below the rising 200-hour moving average at 0.6987. The rising 100-hour moving average at 0.69815 also helped underpin the price. Since then, the AUDUSD has bounced and is now once again testing the key 38.2% retracement level at 0.7022.

So yes, it has been a rollercoaster week. However, despite all the twists and turns, the technical picture still leans modestly in favor of the bulls as long as the pair remains above its 100- and 200-hour moving averages. A sustained move above the 38.2% retracement at 0.7022 would strengthen that bullish case and have traders targeting the 100-day moving average at 0.7052. A break above that level would hand buyers even greater control.

On the other hand, a move back below the 200- and 100-hour moving averages would shift the bias back toward the sellers and signal that another leg lower may be underway.

For now, keep your hands inside the car—the ride remains volatile, but the key technical levels continue to provide the roadmap.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD buyers reverse the declines from yesterday. MA resistance looms above.
item.description:
The USDCAD is moving higher today, reversing the declines from both yesterday and Wednesday. Recall that yesterday's weakness came as the U.S. dollar sold off broadly in sympathy with the sharp decline in USDJPY amid intervention speculation. That selling pressure came despite Treasury yields moving higher following the FOMC decision.

Today, yields are climbing again, with the 2-year Treasury yield up 6.2 basis points and the 10-year yield higher by 6.7 basis points. This time, the U.S. dollar is responding to the rise in yields, and the USDCAD is participating in the move.

From a technical perspective, yesterday's decline brought the pair within striking distance of the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the early May low. The price bottomed at 1.3990, just 9 pips above the retracement target at 1.39812. The inability to reach, let alone break, that key Fibonacci level was a disappointment for sellers looking to gain stronger control. Until that level is broken, the recent decline remains a normal correction within what has been the broader bullish trend.

Today's rebound has lifted the pair to 1.4057, leaving it just 14 pips below the falling 100-hour moving average at 1.4071. The 200-hour moving average sits just above at 1.4078, creating an important resistance zone.

For buyers to take back control, they need to push the price above both moving averages and, just as importantly, keep it there. A sustained move above those levels would shift the technical bias back to the upside and have traders targeting this week's high near 1.4130. That level also marks the bottom of a key floor/ceiling zone between 1.41297 and 1.41488. Earlier this week, the pair failed against that resistance, giving sellers the green light to rotate lower.

For sellers, there is still work to do. They need to force the price back below the recent lows at 1.4003 and 1.3990 and, ultimately, break below the 38.2% retracement at 1.39812. Until that happens, the broader technical advantage remains tilted toward the buyers despite this week's corrective decline.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Logan: Favors a rate hike as inflation is not on a sustainable course
item.description:
Dallas Fed Pres. Lorie Logan is on the wires explaining her dissent at the FOMC rate decision this week.  She was joined by Fed's Kashkari and Fed's Hammack (all three are regional presidents).  Kashkari and Hammack gave their explanations earlier today. Not surprisingly all 3 are concerned about inflation remaining too high for too long with the risks to the upside.

  • Risks to inflation are to the upside; a "solid" job market is strengthening somewhat.
  • Inflation will likely continue to trend above target unless there is an unanticipated shock.
  • Monetary policy is not restraining the economy, and inflation is not on course to return to the 2% goal.
  • Would have preferred a quarter-point rate increase to better balance the outlook and risks.
  • Modest Fed action in the near term would reduce the likelihood of needing sharper action later.
This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.description:
The US employment cost data rose by a solid 0.9% for the 2nd quarter in a row. In a world of rising inflation, having wages and benefits advance with inflation is the only hope for consumers. Absent that and the consumer falls further and further behind. The good news is that wages increase size you 20% last quarter and 0.9% in this quarter with benefits also rising. Of course it would be better if inflation was lower and wage costs were not rising by near 1% each quarter as there are always winners and losers. The data may mask some workers getting much higher pay while other workers are left behind. Nevertheless, the US dollar has moved higher.

item.title: US Q2 Employment Cost Index +0.9% vs +0.8% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +0.9%
  • Wages q/q +0.9% vs +0.8% prior
  • Benefits q/q +1.0% vs +1.2% prior

The U.S. Employment Cost Index showed labor costs continued to rise at a steady pace in the second quarter of 2026. For all civilian workers, total compensation increased 0.9% in the three months through June, matching gains in both wages and salaries (0.9%) while benefit costs rose slightly faster at 1.0%. On a year-over-year basis, compensation increased 3.4%, with wages and salaries up 3.2% and benefits rising 3.8%.

Within the private sector, compensation also advanced 0.9% during the quarter, as wages and salaries and benefit costs both increased 0.9%. Compared with a year earlier, private-sector compensation rose 3.3%, reflecting a 3.1% increase in wages and salaries and a 3.8% gain in benefits.

Despite continued nominal wage growth, inflation-adjusted wages and salaries for private-industry workers fell 0.4% over the year, indicating that consumer price increases slightly outpaced wage gains.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Kashkari and Hammack explain their dissents at the last meeting. Inflation too high
item.description:
Fed's Kashkari and Hammack are speaking and explaining their dissents at the last meeting in favor of a 25 basis point rate hike, arguing that inflation risks remain elevated and that a series of gradual policy moves would be more effective than waiting until larger hikes become necessary.

  • Dissented at the FOMC meeting, preferring to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points.
  • More recent data center investment has added a new demand element to inflation.
  • A series of supply shocks has been responsible for part of the inflation problem.
  • Increasingly believes monetary policy has a role in addressing successive supply shocks that could lead to entrenched inflation.
  • Monetary policy can look through individual supply shocks, but not an ongoing series of them.
  • Wants to manage the risk of inflation becoming entrenched and would prefer to tighten policy incrementally.
  • If inflation durably fades, a strategy of small steps would allow the FOMC to slow or pause further tightening without unnecessary damage to the real economy.
  • If inflation remains elevated, a series of small policy moves would be preferable to waiting and then concluding that much larger actions are required.
Hammack dissented because she believes policy is still not restrictive enough and that the Fed should move now to bring inflation back under control.
  • Inflation has been too high for too long.
  • Not confident inflation will ease without additional Fed action.
  • Now is the time for the Fed to act to bring down high inflation.
  • The longer inflation remains elevated, the harder it will be to return it to the Fed's target.
  • With the labor market still stable, the Fed should keep its focus squarely on inflation.
  • The current policy rate is not restrictive enough.

Kashkari and Hammack are two of three dissenters.  Feds Lorie Logan is the third and is expected to speak as well today.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The USD is higher to start the NA session. How are the charts impacting trader bias?
item.description:
TGIF. The USD is higher to start the US session which retraces some of the declines seen yesterday after the sharp run lower helped by potential intervention in the JPY (Selling USD, Buying JPY). In the video above I will run through the technical levels in play for 3 major currency pairs - the EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD - and explain the bias, the risks and the targets of each as the North American session begins. 

The biggest catalyst yesterday in the forex was the sharp fall in the USDJPY. Today, the Bank of Japan left its policy rate unchanged at 1.00%, as widely expected, while maintaining that it remains prepared to raise rates further if inflation and economic conditions warrant. The decision itself was largely a non-event, but it came less than 24 hours after suspected Japanese intervention in the foreign exchange market triggered a sharp drop in USDJPY from near 163.32 to a low near 158.00 (and just above the key 200 day MA at 157.93  currently). Rather than building on that move, the dollar recovered following the BOJ decision as the lack of an immediate rate hike reminded markets that Japan's yield disadvantage versus the U.S. remains the level of rates in each country which favors the carry trade. 

The market's reaction highlights an important point: intervention can disrupt speculative positioning and slow the pace of yen depreciation, but it may not change the underlying interest-rate fundamentals. Unless the BOJ accelerates its tightening cycle or U.S. yields move meaningfully lower, rallies in the yen may prove temporary. Yesterday's intervention likely reset speculative positioning and served as a warning to traders, but today's price action shows that monetary policy—not intervention—will likely determine the longer-term direction of USDJPY.

Technically, the 100 day MA is at 160.07 will remain a barometer although the price action today was volatile around the level . That level, the swing low from July 3 at 160.44 and the broken 38.2% of the trend move up from the May low at 160.56 are now upside targets. The high for the day did extend 160.84 which was the 50% of the range from yesterday's trading.  

Yield are higher today across the yield curve with a modest flattening:

  • 2 year yield 4.264% up 3.5 basis points
  • 5 year yield 4.403%, up 3.0 basis points
  • 10 year 4.685%, up 2.3 basis points
  • 30 year 5.221%, up 1.4 basis points

Fed speakers will be in focus today as Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan are all expected to discuss their decisions to dissent at this week's FOMC meeting, where each favored a 25-basis-point rate hike. While their comments are likely to reinforce concerns that inflation remains too elevated and upside risks persist, they should also be viewed through the lens of Chair Kevin Warsh's new Federal Reserve.  Warsh spoke on how the market is doing the tightening but did not favor a tightening.  I can see why there could be dissent given the historical precedent to normally do so. 

Stocks are higher 

  • Nasdaq up 125 points
  • S&P up 1.62 points
  • Dow up 173 points. 
This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: How have interest rate expectations changed after this week's events?
item.description:
Rate hikes by year-end

  • RBNZ: 58 bps (97% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)
  • ECB: 38 bps (68% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)
  • Fed: 34 bps (68% probability of rate hike at the next meeting)
  • BoE: 30 bps (72% probability of no change at the next meeting)
  • BoJ: 27 bps (72% probability of no change at the next meeting)
  • BoC: 16 bps (98% probability of no change at the next meeting)
  • RBA: 14 bps (97% probability of no change at the next meeting)
  • SNB: 9 bps (95% probability of no change at the next meeting)
  • Last week's market pricing here

There's been a slightly dovish repricing almost across the board following more central bank decisions and a couple of key data releases. The piricing for the RBNZ remained unchanged due to lack of significant news from New Zealand. 

On the ECB side, several policymakers highlighted the lack of clear second-round effects and refrained from giving signals on a September rate hike. This led to some minor dovish repricing but today's beat in Eurozone core inflation will keep the September meeting live. 

The Fed left interest rates unchanged with three dissenters voting for a hike. The consensus was that Fed's Logan and Fed's Hammack would prefer a rate increase, but we also got Fed's Kashkari joining the dissenting camp. I guess the fact that Fed's Kashkari is a hawkish member, combined with the roughly 30% probability of a rate hike that was priced in before the release, led to some dovish repricing, even though nothing has changed in the bigger picture. Fed Chair Warsh didn't offer any clues about the next meeting as he continues to limit forward guidance. Therefore, the next big event will be the US CPI report on the 12th of August as the data will likely decide whether the Fed hikes in September or not.

The BoE left the Bank Rate unchanged as widely expected with three members dissenting in favour of a rate hike (Pill, Greene and Mann). The consensus was looking for a 7-2 vote split, but given that Mann has been the closest to shifting vote, it didn't surprise the market. The central bank maintained the non-committal tightening bias. The dovish repricing was triggered by BoE's Governor Bailey after he told reporters to not leave the room thinking that the BoE is edging towards a hike. He then reinforced the message by adding that policymakers are not talking about an insurance hike.

The BoJ held interest rates unchanged today as widely expected with Takata (who’s the most hawkish member) dissenting in favour of a rate hike. The statement was largely unchanged with no hawkish signals. The near-term inflation forecast was revised downward, which doesn’t point to a heightened pace for rate increases. BoJ Governor Ueda didn’t offer any clear policy signal, but he mentioned that they could speed up the pace of rate hikes if financial conditions become too easy. That’s certainly not a problem at the moment as bond yields continue to hover around cycle highs, while the Nikkei is down 13% from all-time highs. The market pricing remained largely unchanged.

For the BoC, there's been a slightly dovish repricing although we haven't got significant news or data from Canada. 

On the RBA front, we got the Austrlia's inflation report for Q2. The data missed expectations across the board with the Trimmed Mean CPI Y/Y coming in 3.6%, below the RBA's 3.8% estimate, giving the central bank room to keep interest rates unchanged for longer. 

Lastly, we saw a dovish repricing for the SNB after a Bloomberg report said that the central bank was set to keep its key interest rate at zero until the end of 2027 before probably starting to raise it, according to people familiar with the thinking inside the central bank.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: ECB's Kocher: Decisions to be based on incoming data to bring inflation back to the 2% target
item.description:
ECB policymaker Martin Kocher reiterated the importance of maintaining a data-dependent approach to monetary policy, warning that geopolitical developments continue to pose risks to the inflation outlook.

Kocher noted that recent weeks have demonstrated how quickly geopolitical events can affect energy prices and in turn inflation dynamics. His remarks highlight a key concern for policymakers as tensions in the Middle East continue to create uncertainty around global energy markets.

He stressed that decisions at upcoming ECB meetings in autumn will depend on incoming economic data with the objective of bringing inflation back to the ECB's 2% target on a sustainable basis.

Today's Eurozone CPI report showed core inflation rising to 2.5%, slightly higher than the 2.4% forecast. Without a clear de-escalation in the Middle East and better inflation data in the next month's report, the ECB is widely expected to deliver another 25 bps hike at the September meeting. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Italy July preliminary CPI +2.8% vs +2.8% y/y expected
item.description:
• Prior +3.0%
  • HICP +2.9% vs +2.8% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.0%

Italy's preliminary inflation data for July ticked slightly higher. According to the preliminary estimate, Italy's headline CPI rose 2.8% year-on-year in July, matching market expectations and slowing from the previous 3.0% pace. The harmonized measure of inflation (HICP), which is used by the ECB to compare price developments across the euro area, increased 2.9% year-on-year, slightly above the 2.8% consensus forecast but down from the prior 3.0% reading.

From a broader perspective, the data is unlikely to materially alter expectations for ECB policy, especially after the Eurozone Core CPI Y/Y beat expectations coming at 2.5% vs 2.4% expected. This will keep expectations for a rate hike in September alive.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Euro area inflation nudges up in July, keeps the pressure on the ECB
item.description:
• July preliminary CPI +2.9% vs +2.9% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.8%
  • July preliminary core CPI +2.5% vs +2.4% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.4%

Headline annual inflation in the euro area is seen climbing slightly in July to 2.9%, moving above the 2.8% estimate in June. However, the more concerning development is a further nudge up in core annual inflation too. That is seen moving up to 2.5% in July from the 2.4% estimate in June.

So, it's not just a case of energy prices moving up as being the culprit here. The breakdown for July shows:

  • Food price inflation +1.2% vs +1.5% prior
  • Energy price inflation +10.0% vs +8.5% prior
  • Services inflation +3.3% vs +3.2% prior

Of note, the monthly rate shows a strong push up in both energy prices (+2.4%) and service prices (+1.1%) while food prices were flat.

All in all, it's a signal to the ECB that they can't quite rest on their laurels when they return from the summer break in the months to come. If the trend keeps as it is in August, another rate hike in September looks to be well on the cards at this rate.

Looking to market pricing, traders are seeing ~66% odds of a rate hike in September next. That is just a mild step up from ~64% earlier this week. By year-end, traders are still pricing in ~38 bps of rate hikes with ~52 bps of rate hikes priced before the middle of 2027.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Stealth intervention causes wild swings in USD/JPY; focus stays on Middle East and next US CPI
item.description:
FUNDAMENTAL OVERVIEW

 

USD:

The US dollar weakened across the board yesterday following interventions from both Japan and South Korea. Throw into the mix month-end flows and you get noisy and volatile price action. The moves had nothing to do with the Fed or economic data.

Looking ahead, the focus will remain on the US-Iran developments and on the next US CPI report, as that could decide whether the Fed hikes in September or not.

The situation in the Middle East has barely changed, although Trump’s rhetoric seems to have softened a bit. Nevertheless, until we get a clear de-escalation, inflation risks will remain skewed to the upside. 

JPY:

On the JPY side, the currency appreciated massively yesterday following a stealth intervention. The moves were also likely exacerbated by a rare South Korea dollar-selling intervention. Throw into the mix month-end flows and you get a very noisy and volatile price action.

Almost half of the gains were already erased as USD/JPY buyers thanked the Japanese officials for giving them much better prices. Without a change in the fundamentals, the interventions will continue to be just clearing events to rebuild positions at better levels. The trend is unlikely to change without a dovish repricing in Fed interest rate expectations or a faster BoJ tightening pace.

On the monetary policy side, the BoJ held interest rates unchanged today as widely expected with Takata (who’s the most hawkish member) dissenting in favour of a rate hike. The statement was largely unchanged with no hawkish signals. The near-term inflation forecast was revised downward, which doesn’t point to a heightened pace for rate increases.

BoJ Governor Ueda didn’t offer any clear policy signal, but he mentioned that they could speed up the pace of rate hikes if financial conditions become too easy. That’s certainly not a problem at the moment as bond yields continue to hover around cycle highs, while the Nikkei is down 13% from all-time highs. The market pricing remained largely unchanged with 67% chance of a hike in October.

 

USDJPY TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that USDJPYdropped all the way back to the major upward trendline around the 158.50 level after Japan’s intervention. The buyers didn’t think twice and leant on the trendline with a defined risk below it to position for a rally into new cycle highs with a much better risk to reward setup. The sellers will need a break below the trendline to open the door for new lows, with the 155.00 handle as the first target.

USDJPY TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, the price is trading right around the major 160.50 resistance zone. This is where we can expect the sellers to step in with a defined risk above the resistance to position for a drop back into the trendline. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into new cycle highs.

USDJPY TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, there’s not much we can add here as the buyers will look for a break to extend the rally into new highs, while the sellers will continue to pile in around the resistance to target the trendline and a potential breakout. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Today, we conclude the week with the US Q2 Employment Cost Index. Traders will also keep monitoring US-Iran developments.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: German unemployment rises by slightly more than anticipated in July
item.description:
• July unemployment change 6k vs 5k expected
  • Prior -1k
  • July unemployment rate 6.4% vs 6.3% expected
  • Prior 6.3%

It points to some softness in labour market conditions in the summer with unemployment rising by 6k in July. That brings the total number of unemployed persons recorded to roughly 2,993,000 people.

But perhaps the standout figure is the unexpected nudge up in the jobless rate, moving back up to 6.4%. That is the highest since April, which at the time was the highest since July 2020. So, that arguably points to softer conditions overall as economic conditions in Europe's largest economy remains benign at best since the turn of the year. Naturally, the added struggles from the uncertainty caused by the Middle East conflict is not helping with the situation.

The German labour office notes that: "Unemployment and underemployment are rising noticeably in July, primarily due to seasonal factors. Overall, the weak trend observed in the labour market over recent months is continuing."

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold fails to extend gains as traders await the US CPI and Middle East developments
item.description:
FUNDAMENTAL OVERVIEW

 

Gold strengthened following the FOMC decision despite three dissenters voting for a rate hike. The consensus was that Fed's Logan and Fed's Hammack would prefer a rate increase, but we also got Fed's Kashkari.

I guess the fact that Fed's Kashkari is a hawkish member, combined with the roughly 30% probability of a rate hike that was priced in before the release, led to some hedges getting unwound, even though nothing has changed in the bigger picture. The post-decision gains were eventually fully erased.

Fed Chair Warsh didn't offer any clues about the next meeting as he continues to limit forward guidance. Therefore, the next big event will be the US CPI report on the 12th of August as the data will likely decide whether the Fed hikes in September or not.

On the geopolitical side, the situation in the Middle East has barely changed, although Trump’s rhetoric seems to have softened a bit. Nevertheless, until we get a clear de-escalation, inflation risks will remain skewed to the upside.   

Yesterday, gold got a boost from strong selling in the US dollar as Japan and South Korea intervened in the FX market. The moves in the USD/JPY pair were massive. Those flows spilled over to other markets which coupled with month-end trading made for a very noisy and volatile day.

All in all, we are fundamentally in the same position we were before the FOMC meeting, so now it’s just about waiting for the US CPI and the US-Iran developments.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold is breaking above the downward trendline. We can expect the buyers to step in around these levels with a defined risk below the broken trendline to position for a rally into the next trendline around the 4,400 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price falling back below the trendline to pile in for a drop into the 3,885 level next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we can see the price action has been mostly rangebound since late June, and this leaves traders with little to do other than waiting for technical breakouts or fundamental catalysts. The buyers will need the price to break above the 4,200 resistance to gain more conviction for a reversal of the trend. The sellers, on the other hand, will likely step in around the resistance with a defined risk above it to position for a drop into the 3,885 level.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor resistance zone around the 4,120 level where the price got rejected from several times in the past weeks. The sellers will likely step in around the resistance with a defined risk above it to keep targeting new lows, while the buyers will look for a break to increase the bullish bets into the 4,200 resistance. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Today, we conclude the week with the US Q2 Employment Cost Index. Traders will also keep monitoring US-Iran developments.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ governor Ueda says will conduct monetary policy in a manner so as to not fall behind the curve
item.description:
• Will hold careful discussions at next meeting with risks of inflation overshooting more than in the past
  • To analyse risks of Middle East situation, AI demand, FX developments and their impact at next meeting
  • It's not that we can't make policy changes until the data shows complete stabilisation of inflation at 2% level
  • We will still conduct monetary policy in a manner so as to ensure we don't fall behind the curve
  • Underlying inflation is approaching the 2% level, so we can't ignore the risks of it overshooting that
  • Lower sales tax rate is a positive for real income developments
  • Important for government to ensure markets' trust in long-term fiscal soundness
  • Not appropriate to comment beforehand on increasing bond purchases

The BOJ approach has not changed whatsoever for the most part. They still want to keep the door open for another rate hike but the timing and conditions are making it tough for them.

Call it unlucky or perhaps just a case of bad timing. However, they have had ample of opportunities to dig themselves out of this mess in the past two years. Instead, they wanted to play it slow and took a bit too long before finding themselves in the current predicament.

At first, Takaichi's appointment as prime minister was a bit of a setback already and they had to rush to move right before the end of last year. Then, there was the surprise curveball from the US-Iran conflict as they wanted to wait until after the spring wage negotiations.

Eventually, that still allowed them to move again but the trouble and messiness just continues now into 2H 2026.

Even as price pressures are increasing, there is now the bad mix of cost-push inflation in the picture. Adding to that is downside risks to the economy as energy prices continue to hold higher as the Middle East conflict rages on.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: French inflation accelerates in July, reaffirming the broader trend in the region
item.description:
• July preliminary CPI +2.1% vs +1.8% y/y expected
  • Prior +1.8%
  • July preliminary HICP +2.4% vs +2.1% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.0%

It's not a good look with the rise in headline inflation being driven by a re-acceleration in service prices and energy prices for the most part.

On the former, there was a notable bump in prices for accommodation services and communication services. Meanwhile, the latter shows a rise in the prices of gas and petroleum products.

Even on a monthly estimate, headline inflation was seen up 0.6% in July and that is a notable bounce from the -0.3% estimate in June. So much for hope that the ceasefire deal between the US and Iran at the end of June will provide a brief respite. It just isn't showing up in the numbers here, as well as that across the region so far.

Inflation estimates for Spain and Germany also reaffirm stronger price pressures in July. And that will just add more pressure for the ECB to act next in September in raising interest rates further.

Circling back to the report above, the breakdown shows food prices holding steady at 0.9% in July - similar to last month. Meanwhile, energy prices were seen nudging up to 12.4% compared to 11.0% in the month before. And services inflation was also seen climbing back up in July to 2.3%, up from 1.9% in June.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ governor Ueda says to expect to keep raising interest rates in response to economic, financial conditions
item.description:
• Japan's economy expected to keep growing moderately
  • There is a risk that underlying inflation will deviate upwaard to level above the 2% mark
  • BOJ expected to keep raising interest rates, adjusting degree of easing
  • This will be in response to economy, prices, and financial developments
  • To consider timing and pace of rate adjustment while taking a variety of factors into consideration
  • That inclues likelihood and risks of achieving economy, price outlook
  • Necessary to pay attention to FX developments and its impact on economy, prices
  • No comment on daily market moves
  • Need to pay close attention to events in the Middle East and its impact as well
  • Japan's financial conditions remain accommodative even after latest rate hike
  • It will take considerable time until impact of rate hike spreads to economy, pricces more broadly
  • Will aim to sustainably, stably achieve inflation target
  • It is more important than ever to be mindful of risks of inflation overshooting

There's nothing in there that we don't already know about the BOJ and their policy stance. The decision today mainly reaffirms that and he also doesn't really touch much on the latest FX moves, as you would expect.

At the balance, markets continue to expect no change for the next meeting in September. The odds of that are showing ~77% pricing of no change to the BOJ policy rate. However, things do shift when we get to October pricing afterwards. In entering Q4, traders are pricing in ~64% odds of a rate hike for the October meeting with ~25 bps of rate hikes priced by year-end for now.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What are the main events for today?
item.description:
EUROPEAN SESSION

In the European session, the main highlight is the Eurozone Flash CPI report. The headline CPI Y/Y is expected at 2.9% vs 2.8% prior, while the Core Y/Y measure is seen at 2.4% vs 2.4% prior. The ECB will likely want to see benign inflation figures in this and the next report to hold off from raising interest rates at the next meeting in September.

In fact, in the usual post-meeting "leaks", the ECB signalled that it's ready to hike rates in September unless the inflation outlook improved markedly. This means that the bar for a rate hike is low. Better core inflation figures and a de-escalation in the Middle East is what the ECB is hoping for. Right now, the market is pricing in a 68% chance of a rate hike in September with a total of 36 bps of tightening expected by year-end.

AMERICAN SESSION

In the American session, we have the US Q2 Employment Cost Index (ECI) and the final University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment index. The focus will be on the ECI as that's the most comprehensive report on wage growth and the Fed watches it closely. The only drawback is that it's not as timely as the Average Hourly Earnings data. The ECI is expected to tick lower to 0.8% vs 0.9% prior.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: He predicted the AI infrastructure boom, then leverage cost him control of a $16 billion portfolio
item.description:
What is Situational Awareness, and who is Leopold Aschenbrenner?

Before it became the name of a multibillion-dollar investment fund, Situational Awareness was a widely discussed essay about the future of artificial intelligence.

Leopold Aschenbrenner, a former OpenAI researcher, published Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead in 2024. Across approximately 165 pages, he argued that rapid improvements in computing power, AI algorithms and data-center capacity could make artificial general intelligence, or AGI, possible around 2027.

AGI generally refers to artificial intelligence capable of performing a broad range of intellectual tasks at or beyond the human level, rather than being designed for one narrow purpose.

Aschenbrenner’s argument was not only that AI software would improve. He believed the race toward more powerful systems would require an enormous physical buildout involving:

  • Advanced semiconductors and memory

  • Large data centers and specialized cloud providers

  • Vast amounts of electricity

  • New power-generation and cooling infrastructure

  • Growing investment tied to national security

The phrase “situational awareness” comes from military and tactical thinking. It describes the ability to understand what is happening around you, recognize the forces shaping events and anticipate what may happen next.

Aschenbrenner used the term to describe a relatively small circle of AI researchers and technology insiders who, in his view, understood how quickly AI development was accelerating and how dramatically it could reshape the economy.

He then turned that technological forecast into an investment strategy.

Aschenbrenner established Situational Awareness LP, a hedge fund designed to invest in the companies supplying the chips, memory, data centers, energy and other infrastructure needed for the AI expansion. Its reported holdings included SK Hynix, Micron, AMD, CoreWeave, Nebius and Bloom Energy, alongside a major private investment in Anthropic.

The fund reportedly attracted backing from prominent technology and financial figures and grew to more than $20 billion in assets. Its concentrated AI-infrastructure strategy then produced a reported 439% net return during the first half of 2026.

That extraordinary success is what makes the events that followed so important.

In July, many of the same AI-related investments that had powered the fund’s rise fell sharply. Concentration and leverage amplified the reversal, reportedly leaving Situational Awareness down approximately 67% in a single month and under mounting pressure to raise capital or reduce exposure.

The story is therefore about much more than the collapse of a successful trade. It is about the difference between recognizing a transformative investment theme and building a portfolio capable of surviving its inevitable reversals.

Aschenbrenner may have demonstrated remarkable awareness of where AI was heading. The question raised by the fund’s collapse is whether its portfolio showed enough awareness of what could happen along the way.

The Situational Awareness story is not only about one manager, one AI trade or one distressed portfolio sale. It illustrates several principles that apply to individual investors, hedge-fund clients and anyone evaluating extraordinary investment performance.

1. A good investment thesis and a good portfolio are not the same thing

Investors should evaluate three separate questions:

  1. Is the underlying thesis correct?

  2. Are the assets expressing that thesis appropriately valued?

  3. Is the portfolio structured to survive if the market moves sharply in the wrong direction?

Aschenbrenner may have been right that advanced AI will require enormous investment in chips, memory, data centers and energy. That does not automatically mean every related stock was attractively priced, nor that a concentrated and leveraged portfolio was the safest way to express the thesis.

An investor can be right about the destination and still lose control of the journey.

2. Owning many stocks does not necessarily provide diversification

A portfolio can contain numerous companies while remaining dependent on one economic driver.

Chipmakers, memory producers, neocloud operators, data-center companies and power suppliers may look like different businesses. However, they can all depend on continued AI capital spending, abundant financing and investor willingness to pay high valuations for future growth.

When that common factor reverses, correlations can rise quickly and apparently different positions may fall together.

Investor lesson: Count the number of independent risks in a portfolio, not only the number of ticker symbols.

3. Extraordinary returns should produce more questions, not fewer

A reported 439% return is impressive, but performance of that magnitude should prompt investors to investigate how it was generated.

Possible contributors include:

  • Exceptional security selection

  • Concentration in one successful theme

  • Leverage

  • Options or other nonlinear exposures

  • Illiquid assets whose valuations do not change continuously

  • A market regime that strongly favored the portfolio

A 400% return does not, by itself, mathematically prove that leverage was used. It does indicate that the portfolio probably carried unusual exposure to one or more powerful risk factors. In this case, reporting suggested that substantial leverage and concentration were both involved.

The correct due-diligence question is not simply, “How much did the fund make?” It is, “What risks had to be accepted to produce that return?”

4. Leverage changes a temporary decline into a possible survival event

A cash investor who owns a stock that falls 40% may be able to wait several years for a recovery. The investor may be uncomfortable, but no lender is necessarily forcing the position to be reduced.

A fund using substantial borrowed money operates under different rules. Falling asset prices reduce the fund’s equity while lenders may demand more collateral, impose tighter financing terms or require lower exposure.

That means leverage does more than increase losses. It can transfer control over the investment horizon from the portfolio manager to financing counterparties.

What this means: The manager may remain convinced that the assets will recover but still be forced to sell before that recovery begins.

5. Market liquidity and funding liquidity are different

Situational Awareness reportedly owned many publicly traded stocks. That does not mean the entire portfolio could be converted into cash easily.

Market liquidity describes whether an asset can be sold without causing a major price move.

Funding liquidity describes whether the investor can obtain enough cash to meet collateral requirements, redemptions and other immediate obligations.

A fund can own publicly traded securities and still face a liquidity crisis if its positions are too large relative to normal trading volume. Attempting to sell billions of dollars quickly can push prices lower, damaging the remaining portfolio and increasing financing pressure.

This distinction also explains why a negotiated block transfer may be preferable to selling each position through the open market.

6. Valuable private investments are not the same as available cash

Situational Awareness reportedly retained major private investments, including its Anthropic stake.

Such an asset could ultimately prove extremely valuable. However, a private-company valuation does not necessarily produce cash when a fund urgently needs to satisfy lenders or reduce public-market exposure.

Private positions may be difficult to sell quickly, difficult to value precisely and subject to transfer restrictions. A fund can therefore appear wealthy on paper while having limited immediately available liquidity.

For investors, this creates an important question:

How much of the reported portfolio value could actually be converted into cash during a period of market stress?

7. Forced sellers often sell what they can, not what they want to sell

When liquidity becomes urgent, investors may have to dispose of their most saleable assets rather than their weakest investments.

This can produce a painful outcome. A manager may retain less liquid positions while losing control of high-quality public companies simply because those are the assets a large buyer is willing and able to acquire.

The negotiated Citadel transaction appears to have reduced the danger of uncontrolled open-market selling. The exact purchase price and any discount remain undisclosed, but the broader market principle is clear: urgency weakens the seller’s negotiating power.

Citadel had time, capital and operational capacity. Situational Awareness needed liquidity. In distressed markets, that difference can determine who sets the terms.

8. Position size is part of the investment thesis

Investors sometimes treat position sizing as a separate risk-management exercise. It is more useful to see it as part of the investment decision itself.

If an investment theme can reasonably experience a 30% to 50% correction, the position should be sized so that such a decline does not destroy the portfolio or force an unwanted sale.

The stronger an investor’s conviction becomes, the more tempting it can be to increase concentration. But conviction does not reduce volatility, eliminate unforeseen events or change the terms of borrowed money.

A thesis is not truly investable if a normal adverse move for that asset class makes the portfolio insolvent.

9. Crowded trades can fail faster than the underlying thesis

A secular investment theme can remain valid while the associated stocks suffer a violent correction.

If many funds own similar AI-infrastructure positions, a change in interest-rate expectations, valuations or risk appetite can cause several investors to reduce exposure simultaneously. Initial selling lowers prices, which can trigger more deleveraging and additional selling.

This feedback loop can produce a decline much larger than the change in the underlying long-term business outlook.

Investors should therefore distinguish between:

  • A deteriorating business thesis

  • An excessive valuation

  • A crowded-position unwind

  • Forced selling caused by leverage

  • A temporary liquidity event

Those conditions can overlap, but they are not the same.

10. Drawdown mathematics becomes increasingly unforgiving

A 439% gain turns $100 into $539.

A subsequent 67% loss reduces that $539 to approximately $178. The investor remains ahead of the original $100, but most of the spectacular gain has disappeared.

The recovery challenge also becomes much greater as losses deepen:

This is why avoiding catastrophic drawdowns can matter more than maximizing returns during favorable periods.

A strategy that earns less during a boom but preserves capital during reversals may compound more effectively over a complete market cycle.

11. Return sequence matters

Investment returns are path-dependent.

A 50% gain followed by a 50% loss does not return the investor to the starting point. It leaves the portfolio 25% below where it began.

The order and severity of gains and losses become even more important when a portfolio uses leverage, faces investor redemptions or must maintain collateral. A deep loss at the wrong moment can end the strategy even if the assets recover later.

This is another reason average annual returns can provide an incomplete picture. Investors should also examine maximum drawdown, volatility, financing dependence and the manager’s ability to remain invested during stress.

12. Liquidity is not idle capital

Cash can appear unproductive during a powerful bull market. It does not rise alongside the best-performing stocks, and it may reduce short-term returns.

During a crisis, however, liquidity becomes an active strategic asset. It allows an investor to:

  • Meet obligations without selling core positions

  • Avoid accepting distressed prices

  • Hold through temporary volatility

  • Purchase assets from forced sellers

  • Negotiate from strength rather than urgency

Citadel’s advantage was not necessarily superior knowledge of the ultimate future of AI. Its immediate advantage was having the capital and infrastructure required to transact when another investor could not wait.

13. Risk governance must be strong enough to constrain conviction

Exceptional intelligence and industry knowledge can identify opportunities. They do not replace portfolio controls.

A durable investment operation still requires limits on:

  • Total leverage

  • Single-theme concentration

  • Position size

  • Counterparty dependence

  • Illiquid exposure

  • Drawdowns

  • Collateral requirements

  • The speed at which positions can realistically be sold

The purpose of these limits is not to prevent a talented investor from expressing conviction. It is to prevent one highly convincing thesis from threatening the survival of the entire organization.

The most important risk rule is often the one that still applies when the manager feels most certain.

Questions investors should ask before chasing exceptional fund returns

The Situational Awareness episode also provides a practical due-diligence checklist:

Prestigious backers, advanced technology and impressive historical performance cannot answer these questions on their own.

The AI age does not repeal investment mathematics

There is a sharp irony in this story. The author of Situational Awareness may have demonstrated exceptional awareness of AI’s technological trajectory while showing insufficient awareness of portfolio survival risk.

That does not make the AI thesis wrong. It shows that identifying the future and financing the journey toward that future are separate skills.

Markets reward more than intelligence and prediction. They reward patience, position sizing, liquidity, risk controls and the ability to remain solvent when a compelling theme suffers a violent reversal.

AI may improve research, forecasting, data analysis and trade execution. Future systems may identify opportunities that human investors would miss. But neither AI nor extraordinary human talent can repeal the mathematics of leverage and drawdowns.

Huge potential returns mean huge risks. There is no free lunch.

A firm capable of gaining more than 400% can also be carrying the concentration and leverage that expose it to losing two-thirds of its value when the market turns. The exact numbers will differ from case to case, but the principle will not.

Aschenbrenner may still prove right about advanced AI. In July 2026, however, Citadel possessed the asset that mattered most: liquidity.

The lasting lesson for investors is simple: being right about the future is valuable, but surviving long enough to benefit from it is essential.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UK annual house price growth slows in July - Nationwide
item.description:
• July Nationwide house prices +0.1% vs +0.1% m/m expected
  • Prior 0.0%
  • July Nationwide house prices +1.8% vs +1.9% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.2%

UK house price growth remains a little subdued in July, with the monthly estimate showing a marginal increase while the annual growth slows further to 1.8%. The average price of a dwelling in the UK is now seen at £277,542 from Nationwide's measure.

Overall, there is a bit of softness in the market but that is not all too surprising given recent economic uncertainty from the Middle East conflict as well as some political shenanigans in the UK. But as a whole, the market remains rather resilient still with house prices still keeping higher compared to the same period last year.

Nationwide notes that:

"Market activity and house prices have remained soft in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop. Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict between Iran and the US again exerting upward pressure on energy prices and market interest rates in recent weeks. Financial market expectations for the future path of Bank Rate have been volatile, reflecting shifting views about the inflationary implications of events at home and abroad.

Despite the ongoing risks from the latest energy price shock, the Monetary Policy Committee can take some comfort from the fact that consumer price inflation declined further in June. Signs that wage growth has continued to ease gives policymakers more breathing space to assess the extent to which tighter policy is necessary to ensure inflation returns to target."

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
